newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Lucky breaks in Venezuelan quake tragedy.
newsitem.headline: Lucky breaks in Venezuelan quake tragedy.

text.p: Dragging his feet and complaining of a cold, 15-year-old Oscar Rodgriguez arrived late at this tiny Venezuelan town's high school to take his end-of-term exams -- a delay that saved his life.
"I wasn't even going to go but a teacher convinced me and when I got there the school was moving as if it were on a wave," he told a Reuters correspondent between tears.

Most of his classmates, and his chemistry teacher Pedro Salazar, were killed on Wednesday when the Raimundo Martinez Centeno high school crumbled in Venezuela's strongest earthquake in three decades. At least 20 students died when the school's roof and walls caved in, crushing pupils at their exam desks and severing their limbs.

Civil Defence workers struggling to rescue survivors said the building's complete collapse suggested chronic structural weakness, while horrified neighbours said students had protested for years about the building's condition. "But nobody paid attention," a weeping Mercedes de Guerra said.

Caricao's 13,000 survivors combed the school's debris for lost children. The quake at 3:25 pm EDT (1725 GMT) on Wednesday, which measured 6.9 on the Richter scale, killed at least 41 people in the town, split streets, flattened houses and snapped power and water lines.

Security guard Alcides Amaragua, who narrowly escaped when a local bank "folded in on itself as if it were bombed," said he did not know whether to cry in happiness for having survived or in sadness for those who had died.

In the local 30-bed Diego Carbonell hospital, where six doctors and medics have treated more than 500 patients since late Wednesday, Dr. Raimundo Teran stood over the mutilated bodies of a 14-year-old and three other teenagers smashed beyond recognition and bemoaned the lack of supplies.

"This is the heart of the earthquake. Cumana may be the state capital, but this is where the worst has happened," he said, noting that the hospital's floors and small morgue had been sanitized with kerosene for lack of disinfectant.
At least 59 people died and 322 were injured in the earthquake. Officials say while Caricao has borne the brunt, blocked roads have impeded the rescue effort.

In Cumana, 40 miles (65 km) west of Cariaco and the capital of Sucre state, rescue efforts have focused on the collapsed Seguros la Seguridad office building where 11 bodies have so far been pulled from the ruins and 30 people rescued.

Norys de Coba, 43, said she felt born again after she escaped the falling six-floor building. "The world started moving and I felt sea-sick so I ran out ... and when I turned round in the middle of the street and looked back it had collapsed," she said.
